analysis.one_liner: Restricts the consumer financial watchdog's power to penalize 'abusive' practices and blocks monetary penalties when firms show good faith.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would narrow the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 'abusive practice' enforcement standard, has sat in the House Financial Services Committee without any action since its February 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau uses when it penalizes financial companies for 'abusive' conduct toward consumers. It would narrow the definition so companies are only liable if they intentionally and materially prevented consumers from understanding a product's terms, create a presumption that anything disclosed in fine print is 'reasonably avoidable' by consumers, bar the bureau from treating discrimination as abusive, let companies avoid monetary penalties by showing they made a good-faith effort to comply, and give companies that self-report 180 days to fix a violation before the bureau can act. It would also add a cost-benefit requirement to the bureau's rulemaking, restrict where enforcement cases can be filed, and bar the bureau from penalizing conduct that occurred before a company's most recent compliance exam rating.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, lenders, debt collectors, credit reporting agencies, and other companies the consumer bureau polices. The bill raises the bar for proving 'abusive' conduct, adds a good-faith defense to monetary penalties, creates a cure window after self-reporting, and limits the bureau's ability to penalize conduct found in earlier exams. Companies facing bureau enforcement would face fewer penalties and more procedural room to contest cases.

how_it_helps.text: The bill narrows the 'abusive' standard so the bureau can only find a practice abusive if it intentionally and materially interfered with a consumer's understanding of a term, or took unreasonable advantage of both the consumer's lack of understanding and the consumer's reliance on the company's own representations [S3].

It creates a presumption that injury from any timely, clearly and conspicuously disclosed practice is 'reasonably avoidable' by consumers, and allows companies to escape monetary relief entirely by showing a good-faith effort to comply, by a preponderance of the evidence [S3].

It bars the bureau from interpreting its authority to include discriminatory practices, requires a cost-benefit analysis for UDAAP rules, and limits penalties for conduct that occurred before a company's most recent compliance rating [S2, S3].
It gives companies that self-identify a potential violation 180 days to cure it before the bureau can pursue legal action, and tolls the statute of limitations in the meantime [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers harmed by confusing or predatory financial products. If a practice is disclosed — even in dense fine print the company knows most customers do not read — the bill presumes consumers could have avoided the harm, and a company's claim of good-faith effort can wipe out monetary penalties even when the conduct was abusive. The bureau's enforcement toolkit shrinks at every stage: narrower definitions, an anti-discrimination carve-out, a cure period, venue restrictions, no alternative legal theories, and a look-back limit on civil penalties.

drawbacks.text: The bill's supporters argue the bureau's existing 'abusive' standard is vague and gives the regulator too much discretion over legitimate products, chilling the offer of financial services; the bill would force the bureau to define 'abusive' by rule and weigh costs against benefits before acting [S2, S3].

The good-faith defense and disclosure presumption shift the burden to consumers: an honest supporter would acknowledge that companies can disclose harmful terms clearly and still escape monetary penalties, and that consumers rarely read or understand complex financial disclosures, which is the very problem the bureau was created to address [S3].

The ban on pleading claims in the alternative forces the bureau to pick a single legal theory up front — unfair, deceptive, or abusive — even when the evidence does not clearly distinguish between them, making cases easier to defeat on technicalities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to regulated financial firms, which gain certainty, procedural defenses, and protection from penalties, while the costs fall on consumers, who lose the main legal tool the bureau has used against the most predatory practices — conduct that traps people in products they did not understand. The bill's cure and self-report provisions give companies some incentive to fix problems, but the 180-day window and the statute-of-limitations tolling also delay accountability. The disclosure presumption and good-faith defense are the most consequential changes: they can nullify monetary relief in exactly the cases where the harm was real but hidden in paperwork.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late February 2025 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which has taken no further action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr introduced the bill on February 27, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1, S5].
Seven Republican representatives have cosponsored it; no Democrat has [S4].
The committee has scheduled no markup or floor action, and no vote has occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the status quo holds: consumers' existing bureau protections remain in place because the bill has not moved, while the financial industry's effort to narrow enforcement has gained no ground. If the bill eventually advances, the gain would shift to banks, lenders, and collection companies facing fewer penalties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms' push has stalled; consumers' protections hold

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.role: Sponsor; House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans, with no Democratic support; the bill has not advanced far enough for a party-line vote to occur.

industries.industry: Banks, consumer lenders, and credit card issuers
industries.note: The bill raises the bar for proving their conduct 'abusive,' presumes disclosed terms are reasonably avoidable by customers, and lets them escape monetary penalties by claiming good-faith compliance. These firms profit from products whose costs are often hidden in complex terms, so weaker enforcement directly shifts risk onto consumers.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: These industries are frequent targets of the bureau's abusive-practice cases; the narrower definition, cure window, and look-back limit on civil penalties reduce their exposure to penalties. Their gain comes at the cost of weaker recourse for consumers disputing debts or credit errors.

The bill strips the agency of authority, adds procedural hurdles to enforcement, restricts its choice of court venue, and requires new cost-benefit rulemaking. Its loss of power is the public's loss of an enforcement shield, since the bureau acts on behalf of consumers with no competing commercial interest.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since the February 2025 referral, no Democratic cosponsors, and the 119th Congress running through January 2027, the bill's most likely path is to remain in the Financial Services Committee. Industry-backed measures narrowing the bureau's authority have historically stalled at this stage without a chairman's push, and there is no sign of one here.
